lessons.title: cgroups v2: CPU, memory and process limits by hand
lessons.goal:
Create a control group, put processes in it and watch the kernel enforce a CPU quota, a memory limit and a process limit.

Why it matters: the limits of every container, systemd service and Kubernetes pod are cgroup files. If you can read and write them, you can verify what a runtime really did.

setup.note: These steps use sudo to create the control group `/sys/fs/cgroup/lab` and remove it at the end. They assume cgroup v2 (the default on current distributions).

steps.title: The cgroup file system
steps.text: cgroups v2 is a single tree mounted at `/sys/fs/cgroup`. Each directory is a group; the files in it are the controls. `cgroup.controllers` lists the controllers (cpu, memory, io, pids...) available there.

run.output: cpuset cpu io memory hugetlb pids rdma misc

steps.title: Create a group
steps.text: `mkdir` creates a group. The kernel fills it with control files. To use a controller in a child, the parent must have it in `cgroup.subtree_control` (systemd already enables the common ones at the root).

run.output: cpuset cpu io memory hugetlb pids rdma misc
cpuset cpu io memory hugetlb pids rdma misc
cgroup.procs cpu.max cpu.stat memory.events memory.max pids.max

steps.title: CPU limit: cpu.max
steps.text: `cpu.max` is `QUOTA PERIOD` in microseconds: the group may use QUOTA of CPU time in every PERIOD. `20000 100000` means 20% of one CPU. We run a busy loop inside for three seconds and read the consumed CPU time from `cpu.stat`.

run.cmd: sudo sh -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/lab/cgroup.procs; exec timeout 3 sh -c "while :; do :; done"'; grep -E '^(usage_usec|nr_throttled)' /sys/fs/cgroup/lab/cpu.stat | awk '{printf "%s %s\n", $1, $2}'

steps.after: In three seconds of wall time the loop got about 600 000 microseconds (20%) of CPU. `nr_throttled` counts how often the kernel stopped it until the next period.

steps.title: Memory limit: memory.max
steps.text: `memory.max` is a hard limit. When the group wants more and nothing can be reclaimed, the kernel's OOM killer acts **inside the group**. `memory.events` counts what happened. We run the memory-eating program from module 15.

run.cmd: echo 50M | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/lab/memory.max; echo max | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/lab/memory.swap.max

steps.under: The `memory.high` file is a softer limit: above it the group is **throttled** and forced to reclaim, but not killed. `memory.low`/`memory.min` protect memory from reclaim. Page cache of the group's files counts too, which is why containers can hit their limit with file I/O.

steps.title: Process limit: pids.max
steps.text: `pids.max` limits the number of tasks in the group, which stops fork bombs. With a limit of 6, the loop below can create only a few `sleep` processes.

run.cmd: sudo sh -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/lab/cgroup.procs; for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do sleep 3 & done 2>&1; sleep 0.5; echo "tasks in the group: $(wc -l < /sys/fs/cgroup/lab/cgroup.procs)"; kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null' 2>&1 | grep -E 'retry|tasks|Resource' | sed -E 's/^[^ ]+ line [0-9]+: //' | sort | uniq -c | head -n 3
run.output:
4 sh: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable
      1 tasks in the group: 6

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: A group can be removed with `rmdir` once it has no processes.

run.cmd: sleep 1; sudo rmdir /sys/fs/cgroup/lab && echo removed; ls /sys/fs/cgroup/lab 2>&1 | sed 's/.*: //'
run.output:
removed
No such file or directory

options: 20% of one CPU (20 ms per 100 ms period)

quiz.q: What happens when a group hits memory.max and nothing can be reclaimed?
options: The OOM killer kills a process in that group

quiz.q: How do you put a process into a cgroup?

options: Stopping fork bombs by limiting the number of tasks

check.scenario: A container's CPU graph is flat at 50% although the host is idle. Which cgroup files do you read to confirm it is throttled?
check.answer: `cpu.max` (the quota, for example `50000 100000`) and `cpu.stat` (`nr_throttled`, `throttled_usec`). A rising `nr_throttled` proves the group hits its quota. Raise the quota or use `cpu.weight` (shares) instead of a hard limit if bursts are fine.

lessons.title: cgroups and systemd; v1 versus v2
lessons.goal:
See how systemd uses cgroups for every service, set limits through systemd instead of by hand, and know what changed between cgroups v1 and v2.

Why it matters: on a modern server you almost never `mkdir` in `/sys/fs/cgroup` yourself; you write `CPUQuota=` in a unit. You must still be able to find the cgroup behind a service.

setup.note: Steps with sudo create transient `lab-*` units that are stopped at the end.

steps.title: Every service has a cgroup
steps.text: systemd puts each service in its own cgroup under a slice (`system.slice`, `user.slice`). That is how it tracks all processes of a service and stops them together.

run.cmd: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/crond.service/cgroup.procs | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "process(es) in the crond cgroup"}'

steps.title: Limits through systemd
steps.text: `systemd-run -p CPUQuota=20% -p MemoryMax=50M ...` creates a transient unit with those limits. systemd writes `cpu.max` and `memory.max` for you. We verify by reading the files of the running unit.

run.cmd: systemctl show lab-limited -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec,MemoryMax | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: Change a limit on a running unit
steps.text: `systemctl set-property` changes the limit live (`--runtime` = until reboot).

run.cmd: sudo systemctl set-property --runtime lab-limited MemoryMax=80M; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/lab-limited.service/memory.max
sudo systemctl stop lab-limited; ls /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/lab-limited.service 2>&1 | sed 's/.*: //'

steps.title: Where the numbers are
steps.text: `systemd-cgtop` shows live CPU, memory and I/O per group. `systemd-cgls` draws the tree.

steps.title: v1 versus v2
steps.text:
- **v1**: one hierarchy **per controller** (`/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu`, `/memory`, `/blkio` ...). A process could be in different groups for each controller; messy and inconsistent.
- **v2**: one **unified** hierarchy; a process is in one group; a controller is enabled per subtree. Safer delegation to unprivileged users, better memory accounting (page cache, kernel memory), pressure information (PSI), and `memory.high`.

To tell which one you have:

run.cmd: [ -e /proc/pressure/memory ] && head -n 1 /proc/pressure/memory | sed -E 's/[0-9.]+/N/g' || echo 'PSI is not enabled in this kernel (/proc/pressure is missing)'
run.output: PSI is not enabled in this kernel (/proc/pressure is missing)

steps.under: Pressure Stall Information (`/proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}` and `memory.pressure` per cgroup) reports the share of time tasks were **stalled** waiting for the resource. It is the best single signal for "this system or this container is resource starved" and is what `systemd-oomd` and Kubernetes use.

quiz.q: Which unit setting limits a service to 20% of one CPU?
How many cgroups can a process belong to in v2?
How can you tell cgroups v2 is used?

options: Time tasks spent stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O

check.scenario: A systemd service reaches 100% CPU and starves other services on the same host. How do you contain it without code changes?
check.answer: Add `CPUQuota=50%` (hard cap) or `CPUWeight=` (relative share) to its unit, and `MemoryMax`/`MemoryHigh`; apply with `systemctl set-property SERVICE CPUQuota=50%` for a quick fix and a drop-in for permanence. Verify in the unit's `cpu.max` and `cpu.stat`.

interview.a: A kernel mechanism that groups processes and applies resource limits and accounting (CPU, memory, I/O, pids) to the group. See [the lesson](#/lesson/38/cgroup-v2-hands-on).

interview.q: How do you limit memory of a service?
interview.a: `MemoryMax=` (hard) and `MemoryHigh=` (throttle) in the unit, which systemd writes to memory.max/memory.high in the service's cgroup.
v1: separate hierarchy per controller; v2: one unified hierarchy with better accounting and delegation, PSI and memory.high. See [the lesson](#/lesson/38/cgroups-systemd-v1-v2).

interview.q: What does a container's OOM kill look like?
interview.a: The kernel logs `Memory cgroup out of memory`, the process gets SIGKILL (exit 137), and `memory.events` shows `oom_kill` incremented.

interview.q: How are CPU limits expressed in cgroup v2?
interview.a: `cpu.max` = `QUOTA PERIOD` for a hard cap and `cpu.weight` for relative shares.
Pressure Stall Information: how long tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O, system-wide and per cgroup.

glossary.def: A group of processes with shared resource limits and accounting.
A cgroup component that manages one resource: cpu, memory, io, pids.
cgroup v2 file with the CPU quota and period.
A systemd unit type that groups cgroups in a hierarchy (system.slice, user.slice).
Pressure Stall Information: stall time per resource.
